domains.name: ThreatLocker Interview Prep
domains.summary: Company knowledge and interview judgment for a Zero Trust endpoint security interview: the deny-by-default philosophy, the product stack, the Cyber Hero service culture, and how to answer the questions interviewers actually ask. Independent prep — no affiliation claimed.
key_points: Founded 2017 in Orlando, Florida — Zero Trust endpoint protection on a deny-by-default model
The stack: Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage Control, Elevation Control, Network Control, Web Control
Cyber Hero MDR: 24/7/365 US-based team with ~60-second average response
Interviewers test motivation, customer-service judgment, homelab depth, and evidence-first thinking
Answer like an operator: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate, explain

scenarios.title: Why allowlisting, not another detector?
scenarios.situation: The interviewer leans in: “We already have an EDR. Convince me in ninety seconds that default-deny allowlisting is worth the operational pain.” Two engineers on the panel run detection tooling today, so the answer has to respect their work while making the prevention case.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest ninety-second answer?
evidence: Signature and behavior engines classify AFTER execution begins — fileless, living-off-the-land, and zero-day techniques execute before a verdict exists.
Default-deny asks one question before anything runs: is this explicitly trusted? Unknown code — ransomware, novel malware, rogue scripts — is denied without needing a signature.
EDR is still valuable: telemetry, hunting, and forensics. Allowlisting does not replace detection; it shrinks what detection must chase by preventing most execution in the first place.
choices: EDR is obsolete — allowlisting detects everything faster and cheaper

Allowlisting inverts the burden: instead of recognizing every bad thing, you approve the known-good and deny the rest by default, which stops fileless and zero-day execution that detectors must observe first; EDR then focuses on a much smaller, higher-signal workload
Allowlisting is mainly a compliance checkbox that looks good in audits
Both approaches are identical; the choice is just vendor preference
scenarios.why: This answer states the philosophical core — deny-by-default shifts the problem from enumerating badness, which can never be complete, to approving known-good, which is finite — while respecting the panel’s EDR expertise instead of dismissing it. Interviewers at a Zero Trust company listen for exactly that framing: prevention first, detection as the backstop.
scenarios.hint: Which list is smaller: everything malicious that could ever exist, or everything this business needs to run?

scenarios.title: “What do you know about us?”
scenarios.situation: “Walk me through what you know about ThreatLocker.” The hiring manager wants specifics, not slogans. You have sixty seconds before they move on, and they can tell instantly who did the homework.
evidence: Founded 2017 in Orlando, Florida by Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), and John Carolan.
Zero Trust endpoint platform built on deny-by-default; sold heavily through the MSP channel to 70,000+ organizations.
Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage Control, Elevation Control, Network Control, Web Control, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
$190M Series F in July 2026; a free six-week Zero Trust Cybersecurity Bootcamp; the annual Zero Trust World conference in Orlando.
choices: They are an antivirus company from California that sells to consumers

Founded 2017 in Orlando: a Zero Trust endpoint platform on deny-by-default — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage, Elevation, and Network Control plus the Cyber Hero MDR team — sold through MSPs to 70,000+ organizations, fresh off a $190M Series F
They make firewalls and VPNs for large enterprises
A startup with no public funding history or community programs
scenarios.why: Concrete facts — founding year and city, the deny-by-default model, the product names, the MSP channel, a recent milestone — signal homework. Vague praise or wrong facts (consumer AV, California, firewalls) signal the opposite, and interviewers keep score.
scenarios.hint: Name the year, the city, the philosophy, and at least three products.

scenarios.title: Explain Ringfencing to a CFO
scenarios.situation: The panel asks you to explain Ringfencing to a non-technical executive in under a minute. The CFO cares about risk and cost, not process trees or API hooks. Everyone in the room will remember whether you translated or lectured.
evidence: Ringfencing constrains what an ALLOWED application may do: which other apps it can launch, which files and registry keys it can touch, and where on the network it can go.
Most ransomware does not arrive as malware — it hijacks trusted tools like Word or PowerShell. Ringfencing keeps those tools on a leash.
“Word is allowed to run, but it may not launch PowerShell, read the credential store, or phone home — so a hijacked Word cannot become ransomware.”
choices: Ringfencing is a kernel-level API-hooking framework that intercepts NT syscalls via a minifilter driver and evaluates IRP_MJ_CREATE operations against a policy DAG…

Word is allowed to run, but Ringfencing keeps it on a leash: it cannot launch PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — so even a compromised Word cannot turn into ransomware, which is how most modern attacks actually start
Ringfencing blocks all Microsoft Office applications for security
Ringfencing is the same thing as antivirus signatures, just renamed
scenarios.why: Executives buy outcomes, not mechanisms. The winning answer translates the four restriction dimensions into one vivid business image — a trusted tool on a leash — and ties it to how attacks really work. Jargon-first answers lose the room; wrong answers (blocking Office entirely) lose the interview.
scenarios.hint: If the CFO remembers one sentence after you leave, what should it be?

scenarios.title: The local-admin request
scenarios.situation: A department head asks IT to make her whole team local admins “to stop the UAC prompts.” The ticket lands with you ten minutes before the panel’s scenario round, and you know they will ask how you handled it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the Zero Trust answer?
evidence: Permanent local-admin rights turn every compromised account into a domain-wide incident; most privilege escalation starts from standing admin.
Just-in-time elevation grants a SPECIFIC approved application admin rights for a specific user, time-boxed — no admin credentials exposed, no standing rights restored.
An elevated app can spawn other tools. Ringfence the elevated process so it cannot hop to PowerShell or cmd.
choices: Grant local admin to the team — productivity first, audit later
Refuse outright and close the ticket with no alternative

Offer just-in-time Elevation Control: elevate only the approved application they actually need, time-boxed, with the elevated process ringfenced against hopping to PowerShell or cmd — and every elevated session logged
Tell them to disable UAC on their machines
scenarios.why: The Zero Trust move is least privilege with usability preserved: scope the elevation to the app, bound it in time, ringfence it, and audit it. Blanket admin restores the exact risk the company exists to remove; a flat refusal without an alternative fails the service test the panel is also scoring.
scenarios.hint: What does the team actually need — admin rights, or one app that runs elevated?

scenarios.title: The angry customer wants the policy off
scenarios.situation: A customer on a support call demands you disable the blocking policy “right now” because payroll software is frozen on twelve machines. Their tone is rising. You can see the deny events in Unified Audit: the updater’s child MSI is unsigned and unmatched by any rule.
evidence: Unified Audit shows exactly what was denied and why: the updater’s child MSI is unsigned and unmatched by any rule.
The customer is not wrong to be upset — payroll is down. Empathy and a timeline rebuild trust faster than defensiveness.
Disabling the policy to clear the symptom trades a payroll delay for an open endpoint. The narrow fix is a scoped rule for the signed updater plus its child process.
choices: Disable the policy immediately to restore service, then re-enable it later

Acknowledge the urgency, give a concrete timeline, use Unified Audit to identify the blocked child process, and apply a scoped rule for the signed updater — validating the install works while unrelated unsigned code stays denied
Tell the customer the block is correct and end the call
Blame the customer’s software vendor for shipping an unsigned installer
scenarios.why: Cyber Hero culture is prevention plus service: translate the technical state into plain language, set expectations, and fix narrowly. Disabling the control solves the ticket and creates the incident; lecturing the customer solves neither. The double validation — good path works, denied path stays denied — is what separates a fix from a bypass.
scenarios.hint: The audit already told you the precise, narrow fix. What does the customer need to hear first?

scenarios.title: “Do we still need the VPN?”
scenarios.situation: In the technical round, an infrastructure engineer asks: “We run a traditional VPN concentrator for remote access. Why would Zero Trust Network Access change anything?” They want architecture reasoning, not a brochure.
scenarios.prompt: Which answer shows you understand the network-control story?
evidence: A VPN concentrator is an open inbound port and a trusted tunnel: authenticate once, roam the flat network. It is a favorite initial-access target.
ZTNA brokers per-session, per-application connections — commonly over port 443 — with no open inbound ports and no implicit trust after authentication.
Network Control is the host-based firewall foundation; ZTNA extends deny-by-default from the endpoint to network access itself.
choices: VPNs are fine; ZTNA is just marketing for the same tunnel

A VPN opens an inbound port and grants broad network trust after one login; ZTNA brokers per-app, per-session connections with no open inbound ports and no standing trust — it applies the same deny-by-default philosophy to network access that allowlisting applies to execution
ZTNA means removing all firewalls
The answer is to buy a bigger VPN concentrator
scenarios.why: The parallel is the point: allowlisting denies unknown execution, ZTNA denies unknown network access. Naming the concrete weaknesses of VPN posture — open inbound ports, flat trust after authentication — shows you think in Zero Trust terms rather than product slogans, which is exactly what the infrastructure engineer is testing.
scenarios.hint: Apply “never trust, always verify” to the network path the same way allowlisting applies it to the file path.

scenarios.title: The unknown updater
scenarios.situation: Approval Center shows a user request: “Acme Updater 4.2” — unsigned, first seen in the environment, requested by Finance ten minutes before month-end close. The hash matches nothing in your catalog. Neither trust nor malice is established.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct triage sequence?
evidence: Unsigned, unknown hash, first-seen, urgent business need. Neither trust nor malice is established — this is a question, not a verdict.
A one-button cloud VDI sandbox can detonate the installer and log AV-vendor flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes before any production decision.
Certificate rules outrank hash rules; hash outranks path. An unsigned first-seen binary earns no standing rule today.
choices: Approve it by path — Finance needs it now
Deny it permanently and close the request
Detonate it in the Testing Environment first, review the risk-center findings, then decide: clean behavior earns a narrowly scoped rule, suspicious behavior earns a deny with documented evidence
Approve the hash globally so nobody is blocked again
scenarios.why: Unknown does not mean malicious, and urgent does not mean trusted. The sandbox turns a guess into observed behavior; the scoped rule gives Finance a path forward without granting a permanent, global exception for an unsigned binary. Urgency never upgrades the rule.
scenarios.hint: You need evidence, not a coin flip. What tool turns “unknown” into “observed”?

lessons.title: Know the company cold: ThreatLocker in sixty seconds
concepts: Founded 2017 in Orlando, Florida — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Deny-by-default philosophy: approve known-good, deny everything else — prevention before detection
The stack: Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage Control, Elevation Control, Network Control, Web Control
Cyber Hero MDR: 24/7/365 US-based team, ~60-second average response
Go-to-market: MSP channel; 70,000+ organizations; $190M Series F (July 2026)
Culture signals: in-office five days in Orlando, free six-week bootcamp, peer-voted “most helpful” awards

example.code:
cat ~/prep/threatlocker-facts.txt
# 2017 · Orlando FL · deny-by-default
# Allowlisting / Ringfencing / Storage / Elevation / Network / Web
# Cyber Hero MDR · 70,000+ orgs · $190M Series F (Jul 2026)
example.walkthrough: Sixty seconds of specifics beats five minutes of adjectives. Keep a fact sheet with the founding year, the philosophy, the product names, and one recent milestone — then rehearse saying it out loud until the numbers come without thinking. Interviewers score preparation, not enthusiasm.

pitfalls: Claiming any affiliation with ThreatLocker — this is independent interview prep about their public concepts
Reciting slogans (“world-class synergy”) instead of verifiable facts
Inventing product details you have not verified — say what you know, flag what you do not
lessons.try_it: Record yourself giving the sixty-second company brief. Play it back and count the concrete facts — aim for six: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone.

lessons.title: Answer like an operator: STAR stories and the triage loop
concepts: STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result — one story per question, two minutes max
The triage loop: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Evidence first: cite the audit or log line before the conclusion
Never disable the control to clear the symptom — fix narrowly
Translate for the audience: executives get outcomes, engineers get mechanisms

example.code:
echo "IMPACT: payroll updater blocked on 12 endpoints"
echo "EVIDENCE: audit denies unsigned child MSI; signer valid"
echo "ACTION: scoped certificate rule for updater + child"
echo "VALIDATE: install works; unrelated unsigned MSI still denied"
example.walkthrough: Write the brief before you speak it. Four lines — impact, evidence, action, validation — force you to lead with facts and close with proof, which is exactly the shape interviewers score. If you cannot write it in four lines, you do not understand it yet.

pitfalls: Answering with opinions before establishing facts
Skipping the validation step in your story — “it worked” is not validation
Badmouthing a previous employer, vendor, or customer to sound decisive
lessons.try_it: Take your hardest homelab problem (can you build a VM? what broke?) and write it as four echo lines. Then explain it out loud in under two minutes.

labs.title: Deny by default, hands on
labs.objective: Walk the allowlist decision end to end: verify a file's hash, record the verdict, and state what stays denied.
steps: Deny-by-default means nothing runs until it is proven known-good. This lab makes that muscle memory.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: sha256sum agent-setup-4.2.exe — the simulator computes the real digest of that input
Compare the output to the published value 03de3a29ed578edc18100f62291feff8b27fe053a41c498ab033c03dbfd2b327 — character for character
Type exactly: echo "agent-setup-4.2.exe : VERIFIED $(date +%F)" — record your verdict with today's date
Say out loud: 'Everything not on the allowlist stays denied.' That sentence is the whole philosophy.

checks.hint: Run `sha256sum agent-setup-4.2.exe` exactly. Compare every character of the output digest.
Run the echo command from step 5, keeping the word VERIFIED in it.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you verified before trusting, recorded the verdict, and restated the policy. That is the allowlist workflow in miniature.

labs.title: Read the log like an analyst
labs.objective: Extract signal from ~/logs/app.log: errors, warnings, and counts — the way a SOC analyst triages.
steps: Analysts don't read logs top to bottom. They filter, then count, then read.
Type exactly: grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log — every error line, nothing else
Type exactly: wc -l ~/logs/app.log — six lines total; you already know two are errors, so the rest is context
Type exactly: grep WARN ~/logs/app.log — warnings are tomorrow's errors
Type exactly: tail -3 ~/logs/app.log — the most recent lines tell you how the story ends (so far)

checks.hint: Run `grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log`. You should see the cache connection error.
Run `wc -l ~/logs/app.log`. Six lines total -- two errors, one warning, three info.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you filtered, counted, and read the tail. Two errors, one warning, latest line a timeout. That is a triage summary.

labs.title: Name resolution before escalation
labs.objective: Work a 'can't reach the share' ticket the operator way: DNS first, reachability second, escalate with evidence.
steps: Half of 'network is down' tickets are name resolution. Prove which half this is.
Type exactly: dig fileserver.corp.lan — check the ANSWER SECTION for an A record
Type exactly: ping fileserver.corp.lan — four packets, watch the loss percentage
If DNS resolves AND ping answers, the network path is fine — the ticket moves to permissions or the share service, with your evidence attached
Type exactly: echo "DNS OK, ping OK — escalating to share permissions with evidence" — write the handoff note

checks.hint: Run `dig fileserver.corp.lan` and confirm an A record comes back.
Run `ping fileserver.corp.lan`. You want 0% packet loss.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — DNS resolves, host answers. You escalated the right ticket (permissions) instead of the wrong one (network). That judgment is what interviewers score.

labs.title: Process inventory and the odd one out
labs.objective: Build a process baseline and practice the 'what doesn't belong' read.
steps: You can't spot abnormal until you can state normal. Capture the baseline first.
Type exactly: ps — read every line: PID, TTY, TIME, CMD
Identify the process that doesn't belong on a standard user build. (Hint: a server process on a workstation.)
Type exactly: echo "SUSPICIOUS: node server.js PID 1337 — investigate before kill" — document, don't destroy
Rule: inventory first, hypotheses second, action last. Killing first destroys the evidence you need.

checks.hint: Run `ps`. Find the PID that stands out — 1337 is not a coincidence.
Run the echo command from step 4 with the word SUSPICIOUS in it.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — baseline captured, anomaly documented, no evidence destroyed. node server.js on PID 1337 gets investigated, not summarily killed.

labs.title: Correlate two logs, tell one story
labs.objective: Practice cross-log correlation: the access log shows WHAT the user saw, the app log shows WHY.
steps: One log is a symptom. Two logs are a diagnosis.
Type exactly: grep 504 ~/logs/access.log — when did the user see the failure?
Type exactly: grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log — what was the app doing around then?
Line the timestamps up: 09:15:02 (user-facing 504) against 09:14:47 and 09:20:02 (app errors)
Type exactly: echo "ROOT CAUSE: app timeout on /api/report, not network" — commit to a diagnosis in one line

checks.hint: Run `grep 504 ~/logs/access.log`.
Run `grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log` and find the timeout.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — user-facing 504 at 09:15, app timeouts bracketing it. Diagnosis: application, not network. Stated in one line, backed by two logs.

labs.title: The elevation decision
labs.objective: Practice the Elevation Control judgment call: investigate the request window, then approve or deny with written reasoning.
steps: Elevation requests are trust decisions. Trust comes from evidence, not from the requester's job title.
Type exactly: grep -n ERROR ~/logs/app.log — what was failing during the 09:14 request window?
Type exactly: cat /etc/passwd — who even has accounts on this box?
Weigh it: errors in the window + an unfamiliar requester = deny until verified. A clean window + a known admin = approve with logging.
Type exactly: echo "DECISION: DENY elevation — errors in request window, verify requester identity first" — write the decision down

checks.hint: Run `grep -n ERROR ~/logs/app.log` to see the failures in the request window.
Run the echo command from step 5 with the word DECISION in it.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you investigated the window, checked the accounts, and wrote a reasoned deny. 'Deny until verified' is Elevation Control done right.

simulations.title: The blocked installer
simulations.brief: Monday 9:04 AM. A sales rep needs client-demo-3.1.msi installed before a 10:00 call. The endpoint blocked it: deny-by-default, unknown file. The rep is escalating. Work it like the real thing.

steps.symptom: User: 'The installer won't run. I need it for a client call in an hour. Just turn off the blocking.'
evidence:
BLOCKED: client-demo-3.1.msi — verdict: unknown (not on allowlist)
User: sales-rep-04 | Host: LT-1188 | Requested: disable protection
options: Disable the protection so the installer runs — the client call matters more
Verify the file's hash against the vendor's published value, then route an allowlist request through the proper channel
Tell the user to find the installer somewhere else online
Ignore the ticket until after the client call
steps.explain: Disabling protection for convenience is exactly what deny-by-default exists to prevent. The operator path: verify the hash (proves the file is what it claims to be), then use the legitimate allowlist workflow. Speed comes from process, not from bypasses.

steps.symptom: The hash matches the vendor's published value. The file is genuine — but it is still not on the allowlist.
evidence:
SHA-256 matches vendor published digest
File: client-demo-3.1.msi — genuine, unmodified
options: Run it now — verified genuine means safe to execute
Submit the allowlist request with the hash evidence and give the user a realistic ETA
Copy it to a USB and run it on an unmanaged machine
Add it to the allowlist yourself with no record
steps.explain: Genuine does not mean approved — the allowlist is a policy decision, not a technical one. The request goes through the channel with the evidence attached, and the user gets an honest ETA. Shadow IT (USB, unrecorded approvals) is how breaches start.

steps.symptom: The user asks: 'Why can't I just install things like on my home PC?'
evidence: Deny-by-default: only known-good executes. Home PCs run allow-by-default — the model that lets ransomware run.
options: Agree that the policy is too strict and promise to raise it
Explain the tradeoff in one sentence: the same control blocking this installer is what stops ransomware, then offer the allowlist path
Quote the policy manual at them
End the call
steps.explain: Cyber Hero service culture: respect the frustration, explain the why in plain language, and always leave the user with a path forward. 'This is the control that stops ransomware on your machine too' turns a blocker into a believer.

simulations.debrief: You held the deny-by-default line under time pressure, verified instead of bypassing, used the real workflow, and turned a frustrated user into an informed one. That is the whole job in one ticket.

simulations.title: The 4 PM share outage
simulations.brief: 4:02 PM. Three users in accounting can't reach \\fileserver\shared. One of them is loud. The last change window was 2 PM. Work it like the real thing.

steps.symptom: Three users, same share, same symptom: 'Windows cannot access \\fileserver\shared.' Started around 3:45 PM.
evidence:
3 users, 1 share, onset ~15:45
Last change window: 14:00 (firewall policy push)
options: Reboot the file server — fastest path
Check name resolution and reachability from an affected host first (dig, ping), then check what changed at 14:00
Reinstall the network drivers on all three machines
Tell users to work locally until tomorrow
steps.explain: Scope first: three users on one share points at the share or the path to it, not three machines. DNS and ping take sixty seconds and split the problem space — then the 14:00 firewall push becomes the prime suspect, not a coincidence.

steps.symptom: DNS resolves. Ping answers 0% loss. The share is reachable — but access is denied.
evidence:
dig fileserver.corp.lan → A record OK
ping → 0% loss
SMB: 'Access is denied' (not 'path not found')
options: The network is fine — close the ticket
Access denied with good connectivity means permissions or share config: check the 14:00 firewall policy push and the share ACLs
Replace the users' network cables
Flush DNS on the server
steps.explain: 'Access is denied' after good DNS and ping is a permissions story, not a network story. And the 14:00 firewall policy push lines up with the 15:45 onset — always check what changed. Evidence narrows; guessing widens.

steps.symptom: The 14:00 push tightened SMB rules and dropped the accounting group's access. You have the root cause.
evidence:
14:00 firewall policy push: SMB rule scoped to wrong group
Accounting lost access at ~15:45 (policy propagation delay)
options: Roll back the entire firewall push immediately
Scope the fix: correct the SMB rule to include the accounting group, verify with one user, then confirm with all three
Leave it — security is more important than access
Email everyone to reboot
steps.explain: Fix with a scalpel: correct the mis-scoped rule, verify on one host, then confirm the cluster. Rolling back the whole push would reopen whatever it was closing. And you communicate the cause — users forgive outages faster when they understand them.

simulations.debrief: You scoped before acting, split network from permissions with two cheap tests, checked what changed, and fixed with a scalpel. That is infrastructure troubleshooting at interview standard.

simulations.title: The elevation request
simulations.brief: A developer requests elevation for deploy-helper-v9.exe — an unsigned binary from a personal file share. 'I need it for today's release.' You own the decision. Work it like the real thing.

steps.symptom: Elevation request: deploy-helper-v9.exe, unsigned, sourced from a personal file share. Requester: dev team, release today.
evidence:
Binary: deploy-helper-v9.exe | Signed: NO | Source: personal file share
Justification: 'needed for today's release'
options: Approve — the release is today and the team is blocked
Deny until verified: unsigned + personal share is two red flags; ask for the signed build from the official pipeline
Approve but only for one hour
Ignore it — someone else will decide
steps.explain: Two red flags (unsigned, unofficial source) outweigh one deadline. Elevation is a trust decision: the fix is not 'no' forever, it is 'bring me the signed build from the pipeline and this is a five-minute approval.' Pressure does not change the evidence standard.

steps.symptom: The developer pushes back: 'The pipeline is broken, that's why I'm using this copy. Everyone does it.'
evidence:
Claim: 'everyone does it'
Pipeline status: unknown — unverified claim
options: Approve — if everyone does it, blocking one person is pointless
Hold the line: verify the pipeline claim yourself, and offer to expedite the official build instead
Approve and report the developer
Escalate to the developer's manager immediately
steps.explain: 'Everyone does it' is unverified and irrelevant to this binary. The operator move: check the pipeline claim directly (sixty seconds), and convert the conflict into help — 'let me get your official build expedited.' Firm on policy, generous with assistance.

steps.symptom: You check: the pipeline is fine. The 'broken pipeline' was a misconfigured local runner on the developer's machine.
evidence:
Official pipeline: HEALTHY
Developer issue: local runner misconfiguration
options: Approve the unsigned binary anyway — you already spent time on this
Deny the unsigned binary, document the decision with the evidence, and help fix the local runner
Say nothing and let the request expire
Approve and note 'exception' with no detail
steps.explain: The evidence closed the case: the premise was wrong, so the request stays denied — documented with the hash, the source, and the verification. And you still help: fixing the runner unblocks the release legitimately. Deny the binary, unblock the person.

simulations.debrief: You treated elevation as a trust decision, held the evidence standard under pressure, verified claims instead of accepting them, and helped while denying. That is Elevation Control judgment at senior-interview level.

simulations.title: The Cyber Hero call
simulations.brief: The phone queue shows a small-business owner, third call this week, 'my computers keep blocking my payroll software.' Frustration is high. You are the Cyber Hero on this call. Work it like the real thing.

steps.symptom: Caller, audibly frustrated: 'This is the third time I've called. Your software keeps blocking my payroll app and my people can't get paid.'
evidence:
3rd contact this week | Issue: payroll app blocked
Business impact: payroll delayed
options: Explain that the blocking is working as designed and they should be grateful
Acknowledge the impact first ('I hear you — payroll blocked is urgent'), then gather the facts: app name, version, when it started
Transfer to tier 2 immediately
Offer a discount
steps.explain: Cyber Hero rule one: lead with the human impact, not the technology. 'Payroll blocked is urgent — let's fix it right now' de-escalates in one sentence. Then facts: app name, version, onset. Empathy first is not softness — it is what gets you the details you need.

steps.symptom: The app is payroll-pro-2.8.exe. It updated Tuesday — the same day the blocking started. The hash changed with the update.
evidence:
payroll-pro-2.8.exe updated Tuesday
Hash changed → fell off the allowlist
Blocking started: Tuesday (matches)
options: Whitelist the whole payroll vendor folder permanently to stop future calls
Verify the new hash against the vendor, submit the allowlist update, and explain the Tuesday connection to the caller
Disable blocking on their machines until payroll is done
Tell them to downgrade to 2.7
steps.explain: The Tuesday connection is the diagnosis: updates change hashes, changed hashes leave the allowlist. Verify-then-allowlist is the fix; whitelisting whole folders or disabling protection trades one payroll delay for an open door. And telling the caller WHY (the update changed the fingerprint) prevents the fourth call.

steps.symptom: The allowlist is updated. Payroll runs. The caller asks: 'How do I stop this happening every update?'
options: Say updates will always break and there's nothing to do
Explain the update cycle (new version → new hash → re-verify), offer to set up the vendor's auto-update channel if available, and summarize what was fixed in one plain sentence
Give them your direct number for next time
End the call quickly — queue is long
steps.explain: Close the loop: teach the pattern (updates change fingerprints), offer the durable fix (managed update channel), and summarize plainly. The caller hangs up understanding their own system better — that is the Cyber Hero standard, and it is what turns a frustrated third call into a loyal customer.

simulations.debrief: Empathy first, evidence always, plain-language explanations, and a durable fix instead of a shortcut. You handled the human and the technical at the same time — that is the service culture interviewers are listening for.

consoleSims.title: Default-deny the workstation
consoleSims.brief: A new workstation joins the fleet. Policy: deny-by-default. Set the INPUT chain to DROP everything, then open exactly one hole: HTTPS (TCP 443) from the corporate network 10.0.0.0/8.

tasks.instruction: Add an ACCEPT rule: chain INPUT, TCP port 443, source 10.0.0.0/8.
tasks.hint: Use the Add rule form: CHAIN=INPUT, PROTOCOL=tcp, PORT=443, SOURCE=10.0.0.0/8, ACTION=ACCEPT.

tasks.instruction: Set the INPUT chain default policy to DROP.
tasks.hint: Open Default policies and set INPUT to DROP. Everything not explicitly allowed must fall through to deny.

consoleSims.debrief: One explicit allow, everything else denied. That is deny-by-default in its purest form — the same philosophy behind application allowlisting, expressed in firewall rules.

consoleSims.title: Allowlist the patch server
consoleSims.brief: Patch Tuesday: endpoints must reach the patch server at 10.20.30.40 on TCP 8443. There is also a stale rule allowing ALL TCP from anywhere — a hole from a forgotten troubleshooting session. Fix both.

tasks.instruction: Add an ACCEPT rule: chain INPUT, TCP port 8443, source 10.20.30.40.
tasks.hint: Add the precise rule first: INPUT, tcp, 8443, source 10.20.30.40, ACCEPT. Precision before cleanup.

tasks.instruction: Find and delete the stale rule that ACCEPTs all TCP from 0.0.0.0/0.
tasks.hint: Look at the Rules table for the overly broad ACCEPT rule (source 0.0.0.0/0) and delete it. Any delete of a rule counts — make sure it's the right one.

consoleSims.debrief: You added the precise allow and removed the forgotten hole. Stale permissive rules are how 'temporary' becomes 'breach' — auditing for them is a habit, not an event.

consoleSims.title: Segment the endpoint VLAN
consoleSims.brief: The flat network has to go. Create VLAN 20 for endpoints, assign access port Gi1/0/12 to it, and save the running config.

tasks.hint: At the CLI, type: create vlan 20
Type: save-config — unsaved changes die with the next reboot.

consoleSims.debrief: Segmented: endpoints on VLAN 20, config saved. Segmentation is deny-by-default for the network — a compromised host can only reach its own broadcast domain.

consoleSims.title: Quarantine the suspect host
consoleSims.brief: SOC flagged the host on Gi1/0/7: possible compromise. Quarantine it NOW: create VLAN 99 (quarantine), move Gi1/0/7 into it, and save. Speed matters — but so does not breaking the switch.

tasks.hint: Type: assign port Gi1/0/7 vlan 99 — the suspect host is now isolated at layer 2.
Type: save-config. A quarantine that vanishes on reboot is not a quarantine.

consoleSims.debrief: Quarantined at layer 2 in under a minute, config saved. You contained the blast radius before investigating — containment first, forensics second. That ordering is the interview answer.

terminalMissions.title: Verify before you allowlist
terminalMissions.brief: Helpdesk ticket #4182: a user downloaded agent-setup-4.2.exe and wants it allowlisted. Policy is deny-by-default: NOTHING gets approved without a verified hash. The vendor published SHA-256 03de3a29ed578edc18100f62291feff8b27fe053a41c498ab033c03dbfd2b327. Prove the file matches before anyone approves it.
objectives: Confirm it matches the published value exactly

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `sha256sum agent-setup-4.2.exe`. The output digest must match the published value character for character.

terminalMissions.success_message: Hash matches — the installer is genuine. Allowlist it with confidence. Everything else stays denied: that is deny-by-default working as designed.

terminalMissions.title: Pull the denial lines
terminalMissions.brief: The SOC bridge starts in ten minutes and they want evidence, not adjectives: every ERROR line from the application log at ~/logs/app.log. Pull them now.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log`. You want the lines containing ERROR, nothing else.

terminalMissions.success_message: Evidence first — exact denial lines in hand. That is what the SOC needs, not a paraphrase.

terminalMissions.title: Is it DNS or is it down?
terminalMissions.brief: Ticket: 'Can't reach the file share — is the network down?' Rookie move: escalate immediately. Operator move: check name resolution first, then reachability. The share is fileserver.corp.lan.

checks.hint: Run `dig fileserver.corp.lan`. Look for the ANSWER SECTION — a returned A record means DNS is fine.
Run `ping fileserver.corp.lan`. Zero percent packet loss means the host is reachable — the problem is elsewhere.

terminalMissions.success_message: DNS resolves and the host answers. Not a network outage — escalate with evidence, pointing at permissions or the share service itself.

terminalMissions.title: Inventory before you touch
terminalMissions.brief: A user reports 'the laptop is slow.' Policy: inventory running processes BEFORE changing anything, so you have a baseline. List every process.

checks.hint: Run `ps` (or `ps aux`). Read every line — one of these processes does not belong on a standard build.

terminalMissions.success_message: Baseline captured: bash, app.py, and an unexpected node server.js. You now have evidence to ask about — remediation starts from inventory, never from guesses.

terminalMissions.title: Offboard with a verified list
terminalMissions.brief: Offboarding ticket: a contractor's last day was Friday. Before disabling anything, verify exactly which accounts exist on this box. Dump the account database.

checks.hint: Run `cat /etc/passwd`. Every line is an account — read them all before you disable anything.

terminalMissions.success_message: Account list verified: root plus the candidate account. Offboarding starts from a verified list, never from memory.

terminalMissions.title: Check the window before you approve
terminalMissions.brief: Elevation Control queued requests from 09:14 this morning. Approving blind is how incidents happen: pull the ERROR lines WITH line numbers from ~/logs/app.log and read what was failing in that window.
objectives: Extract ERROR lines with line numbers from ~/logs/app.log

checks.hint: Run `grep -n ERROR ~/logs/app.log`. The -n flag adds line numbers — you need to cite exactly where each failure sits.

terminalMissions.success_message: Two errors at 09:14:47 and 09:20:02, both around the elevation window. Now your approve/deny decision is evidence-backed — that is what the interview panel wants to hear.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the blast radius
terminalMissions.brief: A Ringfence-style policy limits app.py to its own directory. Before you sign off on the policy, verify what the app actually does — read ~/app.py and confirm it stays in its lane.
objectives: Read ~/app.py and confirm its behavior is contained

checks.hint: Run `cat ~/app.py`. Read the whole file — you are looking for anything that reaches outside its own directory (network, shell, file writes).

terminalMissions.success_message: Contained: a greeting function and a loop, no network, no shell, no writes. The policy matches reality — Ringfencing is deny-by-default applied to behavior, and you verified it by reading code.

terminalMissions.title: Two logs, one story
terminalMissions.brief: The 504 on /api/report at 09:15 — app failure or network failure? Correlate: pull the 504 line from ~/logs/access.log AND the matching timeout from ~/logs/app.log. One story, two sources.
objectives: Find the 504 in the access log

checks.hint: Run `grep 504 ~/logs/access.log`. Find the exact timestamp of the failed request.
Run `grep timeout ~/logs/app.log`. Match it against the 504 timestamp — cause lives in the application log.

terminalMissions.success_message: Correlated: 504 at 09:15:02, app timeout at 09:20:02 on the same endpoint. The app hung — not the network. Two log lines, one story: that is triage.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?
